name: Photo lighting / golden hour
lead: Golden hour is the period shortly after sunrise or before sunset when daylight is redder and softer than at midday. Photographers use it because low sun passes through more atmosphere, lowering contrast and weakening direct light.[1]

Wikipedia says the period is often preferred for portraits when warm, diffuse light is wanted, because shadows are less dark and highlights less likely to blow out.[1] In looksmaxxing and style circles, soft side, window or golden-hour light is described as a way to make a face look better in photographs.
No studies were found testing lighting choice on perceived attractiveness; the Wikipedia article itself does not claim golden hour flatters skin or faces.
infobox: Shortly after sunrise or before sunset[1]

paras: Golden hour, also called magic hour, features longer shadows and warm colour. Midday sun, by contrast, produces strong highlights and dark shadows that often call for fill flash.[1]

Photo-presentation advice in appearance communities commonly recommends soft directional light, such as window light or evening sun, for profile and social photos. Proponents say softer light reduces harsh shadows under the eyes and on the jaw. No community sources were available to quote directly.

lore.intro: Soft or golden light is a common suggestion in photo-presentation advice.

claims.claim: Soft golden-hour light makes faces look more attractive in photos
claims.believers: Proponents say the low, warm light softens shadows and skin texture.
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes lower contrast and less harsh shadows at golden hour, but does not make claims about attractiveness.[1] No published study tested the effect on perceived attractiveness.

card.summary: Shooting in soft, low-angle light to flatter your face on camera; physics is clear, the attractiveness payoff is untested.

quick.overview:
Golden hour is the soft, warm light near sunrise and sunset. Photographers favour it for portraits because it lowers contrast and softens shadows.

Whether it makes people look more attractive in photos has not been studied.
quick.mechanism: Low sun passes through more atmosphere, so light is warmer and more diffuse, with gentler shadows.[1]
quick.risks: No health risks. The only caveat is that effects on perceived attractiveness are unmeasured.
